title: What makes a microservice truly "independently deployable" (its own codebase/pipeline, private database, backward-compatible contracts, no shared-library lockstep), and why is independent deployability: not size: the real test of whether you have microservices or a distributed monolith?
shortTitle: What makes a microservice truly independently deployable
keyPoints: Independent deployability means you can build, test, and release a service to production on its own schedule without coordinating with any other service.
Requirement 1: own codebase and CI/CD pipeline so a commit triggers only that service's build and deploy.
Requirement 2: private database that no other service touches, so schema changes never force lockstep deploys.
Requirement 3: backward-compatible API and event contracts so old callers keep working during a rollout.
Requirement 4: no shared-library lockstep where a version bump forces every service to redeploy together.
Independent deployability, not line count or service size, is the real test of microservices vs a distributed monolith.
The test: 'Can I deploy this service alone, right now, without a meeting?'

s1_definition.oneliner: Independent deployability means own pipeline, private database, backward-compatible contracts, and no shared-library lockstep; if services must ship together, you have a distributed monolith, not microservices.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Own codebase and pipeline** – a commit to the Payment Service triggers only the Payment Service's build, tests, and deploy.
- **Private database** – the Payment Service owns its tables; no other service connects to them.
- **Backward-compatible contracts** – old callers keep working during a rollout; use additive changes and expand-and-contract.
- **No shared-library lockstep** – shared libraries are versioned so services upgrade on their own schedule.
- **The real test** – independent deployability, not size, determines whether you have microservices or a distributed monolith.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the Payment department and the Account department are truly independent only if the Payment department can renovate its counter on Monday without closing the Account department too. That means each has its own staff and procedures (codebase and pipeline), its own private ledger (database), a promise that old forms still work while new ones roll out (backward-compatible contracts), and no rule that says 'if head office changes the stamp, every department must change on the same day' (no shared-library lockstep).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Independent deployability means you can build, test, and release one service to production on its own schedule, without a meeting and without coordinating with any other service. Four things make it real: own codebase and pipeline, private database, backward-compatible contracts, and no shared-library lockstep.

At National Bank of India, the Payment Service has its own repository, its own CI/CD pipeline, and its own database. When Pankaj changes the payment settlement logic, only the Payment Service pipeline runs. The Account Service is not rebuilt, not redeployed, not affected. API changes are additive: new fields are optional, old endpoints stay alive until all callers migrate, and Kafka schemas evolve additively through a registry.

The judgment I always emphasize is that size is a distraction. A tiny service that must always ship alongside another is a distributed monolith that pays the network cost of microservices while keeping all the coupling of a monolith. A larger service that releases on its own schedule is a proper microservice.

Remember one sentence: the real test of microservices is not how small the service is, but whether you can deploy it alone, right now, without coordinating with another team.
